originalTitle: Current Ebola outbreak worst ever in DR Congo, WHO says
title: Helping Our Friends in Congo: A Story About Staying Safe!
content:
Hello everyone! Your friendly news reporter for Africa is here with some very important news today. We are going to talk about a country called the Democratic Republic of Congo. It's in Africa, just like many of you! Sometimes, people there get a sickness called Ebola. It's a very tricky sickness, and right now, it's making many people unwell in some places.

What is Ebola?

Ebola is like a very, very strong flu. It makes people feel very tired, gives them a high temperature (fever), and can make their tummy hurt. Sometimes, it can make people very, very sick, much worse than a normal cold or flu. **Did you know?** Ebola is named after a river in Congo! That's where doctors first learned about this sickness many, many years ago.

Where is This Happening?

This sickness is happening in a country called the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DR Congo for short. It's a beautiful country in the middle of Africa, with big green forests and amazing animals like gorillas and okapis. Right now, some towns and villages in DR Congo are having a very hard time because of Ebola. It's important to remember that it's not happening everywhere in Congo, but in specific places that are working hard to stop it.

How Many People are Sick?

Many people have gotten sick from Ebola. It's a very sad time for them and their families. Sadly, over one thousand five hundred people got so sick that they couldn't get better. That's a very big number, like counting all the children in many, many schools. These people were mothers, fathers, brothers, and sisters. It makes everyone's heart feel heavy. **Simple Explanation:** When doctors talk about a 'strain' of Ebola, it just means a type of the sickness. Like there are different types of apples, there can be different types of sicknesses. This type of Ebola is very strong and hard to fight.

Why is This Sickness So Tricky?

Doctors and scientists are working very, very hard to fight Ebola and help sick people. But right now, there is no special approved medicine, like a pill or a special drink, that can make it go away completely and quickly. There's also no approved 'vaccine' yet. A vaccine is like a special jab (a little poke) that helps your body build a superhero shield to fight off sickness before you even get it. Imagine a tiny superhero inside you, ready to fight bad germs! That's what a vaccine does. We don't have an approved one for this Ebola yet. **Did you know?** Scientists all over the world are trying their very best to find new medicines and vaccines for Ebola every single day! They are very clever and brave.

How Does Ebola Spread?

Ebola spreads when you touch someone who is very, very sick with it. It can also spread if you touch their blood or other wet parts from their body, like sweat or spit. Or if you touch things they have used, like their clothes or blankets, without washing your hands very well. It's not like a cold where a sneeze from far away can make you sick. You need to be very close to a sick person or their things to get it.

How Can We Stay Safe and Help?

The most important thing for everyone to do is to **wash your hands!** Use soap and clean water. Make sure to rub your hands together for a long time, like when you sing 'Happy Birthday' twice. Wash your hands before you eat, after you play, and after you use the toilet. It's super important! **Did you know?** Washing your hands properly with soap and water can get rid of many, many tiny germs that you can't even see! If someone is very sick, it's best not to touch them. A grown-up will know what to do and how to help safely. Always tell a grown-up if you feel sick or if someone you know is sick. They will help you find a doctor. Don't be scared to tell someone. It's very brave to ask for help, and it helps everyone stay safe!

Who is Helping Our Friends in Congo?

Many wonderful people are helping the people in DR Congo right now. They are like real-life superheroes! Doctors and nurses are working very, very hard in special hospitals. They wear special suits to keep themselves safe while they care for sick people. The World Health Organization (WHO) is a big group that helps countries all over the world with health problems. They are sending helpers and supplies to Congo. Other countries are also sending money and smart people to help find ways to stop the sickness and make people better. They are all working together, like a big team, to make things better in DR Congo!

What Are the Helpers Doing?

They are taking care of people who are sick, giving them clean water and food to help them feel stronger. They are teaching everyone how to stay safe and clean, like how to wash hands and not share things that might have germs. They are also looking for everyone who might have touched a sick person, so they can check on them and keep them safe too. They are trying out new medicines, very carefully, to see if they can help sick people get better faster. It's a very big job, but everyone is working together with kindness and strength.

A Message of Hope and Bravery

Even though this sickness is tricky and makes many people sad, there is lots of hope! Many clever people are working day and night to find a proper cure and a vaccine to protect everyone. People are learning more and more about Ebola every single day, which helps them fight it better. And most importantly, people are helping each other with big hearts and strong hands. We can all be brave by washing our hands, listening to our grown-ups, and being kind to others. When we help each other and stay safe, we make our world a safer, happier place for everyone, especially for our friends in DR Congo!
summary: A very tricky sickness called Ebola is making many people unwell in parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and while many good people are helping, there isn't a special medicine or jab for it yet, so washing hands and listening to grown-ups is very important to stay safe.
whyMatters: This is important because we care about our friends and family in Africa, and learning about Ebola helps us understand how to keep ourselves and our communities healthy and safe from sicknesses, showing we are all part of one big family.
